cards.front: A prolonged aPTT in haemophilia [___] on mixing with normal plasma, unlike an inhibitor.
cards.context:
Both haemophilias sit in the INTRINSIC pathway, which aPTT measures. PT/INR tests the extrinsic pathway and is untouched.

So the coagulation screen shows an isolated prolonged aPTT — and because the defect is a factor rather than an inhibitor, it CORRECTS on mixing with normal plasma.

A prolonged aPTT that fails to correct points at an inhibitor, such as antiphospholipid antibody, instead.

cards.front: A well child with a runny nose is due MMR today. The cold is not a reason to [___] the vaccine.
cards.context:
A runny nose in an otherwise well child is not a reason to move a live vaccine to next year.

Delay is for a significant fever or a real contraindication. A missed visit is how measles immunity slips.

cards.front: A child's eczema flare has settled after topical steroid. The treatment continued over clear skin to prevent barrier breakdown is regular [___].
cards.context:
Emollients repair the skin barrier and continue every day, including when eczema looks clear.

Topical corticosteroids treat active inflammation; they do not replace maintenance moisturising.

cards.front: In febrile neutropaenia, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics must be given within [___] minutes.
cards.context:
A neutropaenic child cannot mount a normal inflammatory response — Gram-negative bacteraemia can progress from fever spike to septic shock in hours.

On arrival take blood cultures (peripheral + central line), urine, swabs, and CXR if respiratory symptoms — do NOT let investigations delay the first dose of empiric piperacillin-tazobactam (or local equivalent).

reference.title: Fever and suspected or confirmed neutropenia

cards.front: The chest radiograph in transient tachypnoea of the newborn characteristically shows prominent [___] markings.
cards.context:
Retained lung water sits in the interstitium and the fissures, so the film looks wet rather than airless.

Contrast this with the diffuse ground-glass and low volumes of surfactant deficiency — the two are distinguished on the same film.

cards.front: Avoid [___] where possible below 41 weeks' corrected gestational age, especially with jaundice or calcium-containing solutions or TPN.
cards.context:
Ceftriaxone can displace bilirubin from albumin and can precipitate with calcium-containing solutions.

RCH advises avoiding it where possible below 41 weeks' corrected gestational age, particularly with jaundice or calcium-containing infusions such as TPN.

Cefotaxime is the usual third-generation alternative when available.

cards.front: Use [___] growth charts for 0-2 years and CDC charts for 2-18 years; serial trends matter more than a single measurement.
cards.context:
WHO 0–2 charts use breastfed-infant data as the reference standard. From 2–18 years RCH uses CDC charts — they are US-developed, and they are still the Australian recommendation, not a US-only rule.

What matters is the trend, not a single value. Crossing 2 percentile lines downward triggers a failure-to-thrive workup.

cards.front: Per RCH, the presence of any [___] in the CSF, at any age, may indicate bacterial meningitis and warrants senior discussion.
cards.context:
Beyond the newborn period the expected CSF neutrophil count is zero, so even a small number is abnormal rather than borderline.

Some studies find up to 5% of white cells in the CSF of neonates without meningitis are neutrophils, which is why the newborn line is read differently.

The action here is escalation, not reassurance.

cards.front: The Paediatric Assessment Triangle gauges appearance, work of breathing, and [___] to the skin — a hands-off, across-the-room read of how sick a child is before any vital sign.
cards.context:
The Paediatric Assessment Triangle is a hands-off, across-the-room tool: appearance (tone, interactiveness, consolability, gaze, cry), work of breathing, and circulation to skin (pallor, mottling, cyanosis).

It identifies the sick child and the type of physiological problem in seconds, before any vital sign is measured.

cards.front: Apart from the hepatitis B birth dose, routine infant vaccination can begin from [___] of age.
cards.context: The hepatitis B birth dose is the exception. Routine infant vaccine series otherwise begin at 6 weeks; catch-up can start later without restarting the course.

cards.front: A newborn in severe respiratory distress whose film shows a bubbly left hemithorax continuous with the abdominal gas, mediastinal shift to the right and a non-aerated left lung has a [___] hernia.
cards.context:
Congenital diaphragmatic hernia is the newborn-with-respiratory-distress film you must not miss, and the appearance is unmistakable once named.

Bowel loops in the chest give a bubbly lucency that is continuous with the gas pattern in the abdomen. The heart is pushed away and the lung on that side is not aerated.

cards.front: Greasy, yellow, adherent scale on the scalp of an otherwise well infant is cradle [___] (infantile seborrhoeic dermatitis).
cards.context: Cradle cap is infantile seborrhoeic dermatitis — non-itchy and self-limiting. Soften the scale with emollient then brush gently; ketoconazole shampoo or mild hydrocortisone if persistent.

cards.front: A testis is palpable outside the normal descent path, between the external oblique aponeurosis and Scarpa's fascia. It lies in the [___] inguinal pouch.
cards.context: An ectopic testis has deviated away from the normal route of descent. The commonest destination is the superficial inguinal pouch, between the external oblique aponeurosis and Scarpa's fascia.

cards.front: Once susceptibilities are known, change broad empiric treatment to a [___]-spectrum agent or stop it if bacterial infection is excluded.
cards.context:
Broad empiric cover is a temporary hedge against uncertainty. Once cultures and susceptibilities identify the pathogen, RCH advises changing to a narrow-spectrum agent.

Also stop antibiotics when the clinical course and investigations support a non-bacterial diagnosis; de-escalation includes stopping, not only swapping drugs.

cards.front: Fifth disease is caused by parvovirus [___], which can trigger fetal hydrops if a non-immune pregnant woman is exposed.
cards.context:
Fifth disease (erythema infectiosum): parvovirus B19 infection.

Three-stage rash: prodromal mild illness, then bright slapped-cheek facial erythema sparing nasolabial folds, then lacy reticular rash on trunk/limbs (may recur for weeks).

Child is no longer infectious once the rash appears. Avoid contact with pregnant women (risk of fetal red-cell aplasia → severe anaemia → high-output cardiac failure → hydrops fetalis).

cards.front: A small pleural effusion first blunts the [___] angle; a larger one tracks upwards in a meniscus configuration.
cards.context:
Volume determines appearance, and the progression is worth holding as a sequence.

A small effusion blunts the costophrenic angle. A larger one tracks up the chest wall in a meniscus, and fluid may also be seen within the fissures.

cards.front: An ex-term 1-month-old with bronchiolitis has persistent SpO₂ of 91% in room air. Oxygen IS indicated — infants under [___] use the higher 92% PREDICT threshold rather than 90%.
cards.context:
PREDICT stratifies the oxygen threshold by age and risk rather than one flat number — the very young, and infants under 12 months with an underlying condition, earn the higher cut-off.

Above the threshold, chasing mid-to-high 90s saturations only lengthens admissions (the BIDS trial); below it, persistent readings — not a single dip — justify starting low-flow oxygen.

cards.front: Most common organism in paediatric osteomyelitis is [___] (>80%); X-rays may be normal early — use MRI or bone scan for early diagnosis.
cards.context:
Staphylococcus aureus causes most paediatric osteomyelitis by haematogenous seeding of the metaphysis. Take blood cultures first if this will not delay treatment.

Plain X-rays exclude fracture or tumour but can be normal early; periosteal reaction and bone destruction take 10–14 days. MRI detects early marrow oedema and any subperiosteal abscess or joint extension.

Start antibiotics while imaging is arranged, then narrow to cultures and step down to oral therapy once improving. Drain an abscess or debride disease that fails medical treatment.

cards.front: Nail shedding weeks after hand-foot-mouth disease happens because the virus arrests the nail [___]; a milder arrest gives Beau's lines instead.
cards.context:
Onychomadesis after hand-foot-mouth disease is a growth-arrest phenomenon: the viral illness briefly halts the nail matrix, and the resulting defect emerges as the nail grows out, which takes weeks.

The nail separates from the proximal fold and is shed intact. The same mechanism, less severe, produces Beau's lines — a transverse groove rather than a complete shed.

Both are markers of a systemic insult some weeks earlier. Nothing needs doing, but the timing is the whole teaching point: parents present alarmed weeks after the child recovered and the connection is easy to miss.

cards.front: Atopic dermatitis affects 10-20% of children, with 85% of childhood cases beginning before age 5. It can precede food allergy, allergic rhinitis and [___], but this is an increased-risk association rather than a fixed progression.
cards.context:
Eczema affects 10-20% of children; about 85% of childhood cases begin before age 5. It reflects skin-barrier dysfunction and a Th2-skewed immune response.

Early or severe eczema is associated with later food allergy, asthma and allergic rhinitis. The 'atopic march' is a population association, not a fixed sequence; most children do not develop every condition.

cards.front: [___] stridor = upper airway; expiratory wheeze = lower airway; biphasic stridor = fixed glottic/subglottic lesion; grunting = airspace pathology.
cards.context:
The phase of the noise localises the lesion.

Expiratory wheeze: intrathoracic small airways collapse as pressure rises — lower airway obstruction (asthma, bronchiolitis).

Biphasic stridor = fixed glottic/subglottic obstruction. Grunting = self-PEEP against airspace pathology (pneumonia, pulmonary oedema, RDS).

cards.front: On a growth chart, short stature means height below the [___] centile for age and sex.
cards.context:
Short stature is not a single diagnosis — it is a pattern on the growth chart.

Plot height for age and sex, then read the centile band. A child plainly below the normal range on the chart is short; Victoria at 105 cm at 7 years sits under the 3rd centile line visually.

The first move is always the chart plus a careful history and examination, not a formula or velocity calculation.

cards.front: After a correction bolus, ketones may keep rising for [___] hours before falling, which is expected rather than treatment failure.
cards.context:
Two ketone trajectories look identical for the first hour and mean opposite things. Expected: after a correction bolus, ketones may RISE for one to two hours and then fall.

That is the insulin working: fat breakdown stops, but circulating ketones take time to clear. Re-dosing here stacks insulin.

Ketones still climbing after that window, especially above 1.5, despite extra boluses, mean the home plan has failed and need urgent review. The first recheck does not tell you it worked; the second does.

cards.front: Joint inflammation in a child under 16 with no other cause must last at least [___] to define juvenile idiopathic arthritis.
cards.context: The 6-week threshold is the whole point — it separates chronic JIA from the far commoner transient/post-infectious arthritis that resolves on its own. Onset must be before the 16th birthday.

cards.front: In ALL, reduced red-cell production causes [___], producing pallor and fatigue.
cards.context:
Every presenting feature traces back to blast cells crowding out normal marrow: loss of red-cell production causes anaemia (pallor, fatigue).

Loss of platelets causes thrombocytopaenia (bruising, petechiae), and marrow expansion causes bone pain.

Hepatosplenomegaly and lymphadenopathy reflect leukaemic infiltration of those organs. Peak age 2-5 years; ~85-90% cured with 2-year multi-phase chemo.

cards.front: The five CRASH features of Kawasaki disease are conjunctivitis, rash, adenopathy, [___] and hand and foot changes.
cards.context:
CRASH is the retrieval handle: Conjunctivitis, Rash, Adenopathy, Strawberry tongue, Hands and feet. Fever is required on top of these, not one of them.

The features accumulate rather than appearing together, so a child seen early can look incomplete and still have the disease.

Conjunctivitis is bilateral and non-purulent, and the node qualifies at 1.5 cm or more, usually on one side.

cards.front: Profuse purulent conjunctivitis beginning on day 2–5 of life is [___] until excluded.
cards.context:
Neonatal conjunctivitis timing reflects incubation: chemical irritation is typical on days 0–2, whereas gonococcus classically presents on days 2–5 with profuse purulent discharge.

Gonococcal disease can perforate the cornea and needs systemic treatment, not topical drops alone.

cards.front: Suspected concussion requires removal from play; [___] same-day return to contact sport, regardless of symptom resolution.
cards.context:
'If in doubt, sit them out.' Second-impact syndrome — a second impact during the vulnerable post-concussion window — causes catastrophic cerebral oedema with high mortality.

Graduated return-to-play: ≥24-48 hours rest → light activity (no symptoms) → sport-specific exercise → non-contact training → full contact (medical clearance) → return.

cards.front: The main differential for the cystic-looking hemithorax of a diaphragmatic hernia is [___] malformation of the lung.
cards.context:
Knowing the differential stops you over-calling a bubbly chest.

Cystic adenomatoid malformation of the lung produces cystic lucencies in the hemithorax without continuity to the abdominal gas pattern — that continuity is the discriminator.

cards.front: Two serious complications of osteomyelitis are spread to the adjacent joint causing septic arthritis, and unequal limb lengths from growth-plate damage, termed [___].
cards.context: Untreated or chronic osteomyelitis spreads to the neighbouring joint and damages the adjacent growth plate, so a delayed presentation risks both an infected joint and a future limb-length problem.

cards.front: A neonate with bilious vomiting on day 1 has a 'double-bubble' on AXR. Approximately 30% of these cases are associated with [___].
cards.context:
On abdominal X-ray, duodenal atresia shows the 'double-bubble' sign — air in the stomach and proximal duodenum, no distal gas, separated by the pylorus.

Always check for a chromosomal association: ~30% of duodenal atresia cases have trisomy 21. The AXR finding should prompt karyotype review and a search for other anomalies (cardiac, anorectal).

cards.front: A 5-week-old settled since birth develops escalating projectile non-bilious vomiting after feeds, then demands re-feeding straight away. Onset inside the [___]-week window makes pyloric stenosis the diagnosis, not worsening reflux.
cards.context:
Age is the hinge separating the two vomiting stories. Reflux is present from the early weeks, effortless, and the baby stays content.

New forceful vomiting that escalates feed by feed in a previously settled infant of this age is outlet obstruction until proven otherwise — examine for the olive and check a venous gas before any feed trial.

cards.front: To achieve a neutral airway in an infant, place a folded towel under the [___] — the large occiput otherwise flexes the neck and obstructs the airway.
cards.context:
An infant's occiput is proportionally huge: lying flat, it flexes the neck and closes the airway you are trying to open.

A folded towel under the SHOULDERS — not the head — restores the neutral position. In an older child the target is the sniffing position instead.

Suction only what you can see, with a light: blind suction provokes laryngospasm and bradycardia.

cards.front: Nephrotic syndrome triad: [___], hypoalbuminaemia, and oedema; often hypercholesterolaemia from compensatory hepatic lipoprotein synthesis.
cards.context:
Nephrotic syndrome triad: heavy proteinuria (urine protein:creatinine ratio >200 mg/mmol), hypoalbuminaemia (<25 g/L), oedema. Often plus hypercholesterolaemia (compensatory hepatic lipoprotein synthesis).

Mechanism: damage to glomerular podocytes → loss of negative-charge barrier → albumin and other anionic proteins leak into urine. The oedema follows colloid pressure loss.

cards.front: Cerebral palsy: [___]-progressive motor disorder from developing-brain injury; prevalence 2 per 1000 live births; spastic is the most common motor type.
cards.context:
Cerebral palsy is a NON-PROGRESSIVE motor disorder caused by injury to the developing brain — the brain injury itself is fixed but motor manifestations may evolve as the child grows. Prevalence 2 per 1000 live births.

Classified by topography (hemiplegia, diplegia, quadriplegia) and motor type (spastic ~80%, dyskinetic, ataxic).

Risk factors: prematurity, low birthweight, perinatal asphyxia, neonatal encephalopathy.

cards.front: Otitis externa affects the ear canal; cardinal clinical sign is pain when pulling the pinna or pressing the tragus — distinguishes it from otitis media, which affects the [___] ear.
cards.context:
Otitis externa is a skin/soft-tissue infection of the external auditory canal — distinct from otitis media (middle ear behind intact TM).

Cardinal sign: pain on pulling pinna or pressing tragus (moves inflamed canal skin) — AOM doesn't cause this.

Topical antibiotic + steroid drops (Sofradex, Ciproxin HC); DON'T syringe (risks pushing infection deeper).

cards.front: A congenital gap in the upper lip from failed fusion of the maxillary and medial nasal prominences is a [___] lip.
cards.context: Cleft lip with or without palate is a common craniofacial anomaly needing staged multidisciplinary repair. Screen for feeding difficulty, recurrent otitis media, and later speech problems.

cards.front: Tumour lysis syndrome metabolic derangement: high [___], high phosphate, high urate, low calcium; prevent with hydration + allopurinol/rasburicase.
cards.context:
Tumour lysis syndrome (TLS) is rapid cell death dumping intracellular contents into circulation, classically after starting chemo for high-tumour-burden malignancies (ALL, Burkitt's lymphoma).

Causes AKI (urate crystals + calcium phosphate deposition), cardiac arrhythmia.

Prevention: aggressive hydration + allopurinol (or rasburicase for high-risk).

cards.front: Asymptomatic labial adhesions in a child who voids easily are managed with [___].
cards.context:
Thin prepubertal mucosa can adhere after minor irritation. Most labial adhesions separate spontaneously as the child grows.

If urine passes easily and there are no symptoms, intervention offers little benefit. Urinary obstruction warrants specialist advice; forced separation can cause pain and recurrence.

cards.front: Emollients benefit atopic eczema chiefly by reducing [___], which is elevated when the skin barrier is defective.
cards.context:
Eczema is fundamentally a barrier disease: a leaky epidermis lets moisture escape, causing dryness and itch.

That is WHY emollients are the mainstay — they seal the barrier and cut that leakage, rather than just relieving symptoms. Topical steroids treat the inflammation on top but do not repair the barrier.

cards.front: The commonest cause of chronic infantile [___] — worse when supine and self-resolving by ~18 months — is laryngomalacia.
cards.context: Floppy, immature supraglottic cartilage collapses inward on inspiration. The classic pattern: an otherwise well infant with inspiratory stridor that's worse when supine or feeding and settles on its own by ~18 months.

cards.front: A central venous line inserted via the subclavian or internal jugular vein passes through the brachiocephalic vein into the [___], with the tip sited at the cavoatrial junction.
cards.context:
Central line tip position is the third line to know on a neonatal film.

The two usual routes both converge on the superior vena cava: subclavian to brachiocephalic, or internal jugular to brachiocephalic.

The target is the SVC at its junction with the right atrium — a tip deep inside the atrium is the commonest malposition and risks arrhythmia.

cards.front: A first episode of wheeze and crackles in an infant under 12 months, usually from RSV, is [___].
cards.context: The defining combination: a FIRST episode of wheeze and crackles in an infant under 12 months, in winter, usually RSV. The 'first episode under 1' criterion is what separates it from recurrent viral-induced wheeze.

cards.front: Bronchiolitis = first episode of viral wheeze with crackles in infants under [___] months; obstruction is dominated by small-airway oedema, epithelial debris and mucus plugging.
cards.context:
A first episode under 12 months supports bronchiolitis: self-limiting viral small-airway inflammation, usually caused by RSV and managed supportively. Oedema, epithelial debris and mucus plug the small airways.

Bronchodilators are not used routinely because trials show no consistent improvement in admission or illness duration — not because infants lack airway smooth muscle.

cards.front: A GP reviews a well, premenarchal 13-year-old girl whose rib hump was found on screening; her neurology is normal. A standing spine X-ray shows a 25-degree right thoracic curve. The GP's next step is [___].
cards.context:
The Cobb angle sets the threshold: a curve over 20 degrees goes to a specialist, while a smaller curve in a growing child is re-examined and re-imaged.

The orthopaedic surgeon then weighs curve size against remaining growth to choose observation, bracing or surgery. Before menarche she is near peak growth, when curves progress fastest.

Reassurance alone is the trap, and MRI is reserved for red flags such as pain, a left thoracic curve or abnormal neurology.

cards.front: In a child with chronic haemolysis, parvovirus B19 causes an [___] by halting red cell production.
cards.context:
The rash itself is harmless; this is when parvovirus IS a problem. B19 infects red cell precursors and briefly shuts down red cell production. A healthy child does not notice, as red cells outlive the pause.

In CHRONIC HAEMOLYTIC ANAEMIA (sickle cell disease, hereditary spherocytosis, thalassaemia), red cells are short-lived with no reserve.

The same pause makes haemoglobin fall abruptly: an aplastic crisis, with pallor, lethargy and a LOW reticulocyte count despite severe anaemia.

cards.front: Pyloric stenosis presents at 2–8 weeks rather than at birth because the pyloric muscle [___] progressively after birth until the outlet occludes.
cards.context:
The pyloric muscle is normal at birth and thickens progressively over the first weeks of life, so the obstruction is acquired — it emerges only once the channel finally occludes, never on day one.

Vomiting from the first day of life therefore points to a congenital cause such as atresia or malrotation instead.

cards.front: The standard EpiPen auto-injector, for a child over 20 kg, delivers [___] mg of adrenaline.
cards.context: Step up from the EpiPen Jr (0.15 mg) to the standard EpiPen (0.3 mg) once a child passes about 20 kg.

cards.front: Acute pulmonary illness can increase antidiuretic hormone secretion, causing the child to retain [___].
cards.context: An unwell child may need less than the calculated full maintenance rate. Reassess hydration and sodium before choosing the prescription.

cards.front: Two healthcare rescuers doing paediatric CPR use a ratio of 15:2, compressing one-[___] of chest depth at 100-120/min.
cards.context:
Healthcare-rescuer paediatric ratio is 15:2, not the adult 30:2. Depth one-third of the chest, rate 100-120.

Infant: two thumbs, hands encircling. Small child: heel of one hand.

cards.front: An alert infant with hypotonia, absent deep tendon reflexes, and tongue fasciculations has a [___] cause.
cards.context:
Low tone with absent reflexes and tongue fasciculations but preserved cognition is a peripheral lower-motor-neuron pattern, classically anterior horn cell disease.

Contrast with a 'floppy strong' infant (hypotonia but normal power), which points to a central cause.

cards.front: Per the Australian Child Maltreatment Study, about [___] in 10 children experience maltreatment; the commonest single type is exposure to domestic violence; health professionals are mandatory reporters in all Australian jurisdictions.
cards.context:
The Australian Child Maltreatment Study (2023, n=8,503) found ~62% of children experience at least one of five maltreatment types.

By population prevalence the commonest is exposure to domestic violence (~40%); neglect is the LEAST common (~9%). The older 'neglect most common' figure came from notification data, not prevalence.

Health professionals are mandatory reporters in all states/territories. Threshold = REASONABLE concern: flag, don't investigate or prove abuse.

cards.front: Monospot test for EBV is rapid and specific but lacks sensitivity — false negatives common in first week and in children under [___]; send VCA-IgM serology if Monospot negative and suspicion remains high.
cards.context:
Monospot detects heterophile antibodies — IgM that EBV infection induces against unrelated antigens (horse RBCs in the test).

Sensitivity is poor — false negatives in the first week (antibodies not yet developed) and in children under 4 (humoral response often skips heterophile stage).

cards.front: A 2-year-old in septic shock remains poorly perfused after 40 mL/kg of 0.9% saline, and now has hepatomegaly and crackles. The next step is starting [___] rather than a further bolus.
cards.context:
Shock that persists after 40 mL/kg is fluid-refractory. New hepatomegaly and crackles say the circulation is now overloaded, and another bolus worsens it.

The inotrope is adrenaline for cold shock (mottled, weak pulses), run dilute through a peripheral line until central access is in.

Noradrenaline is the choice for warm shock with bounding pulses and a low diastolic pressure. Antibiotics should already be running.

cards.front: The confirmatory diagnostic test for cystic fibrosis is the [___].
cards.context: Quantitative pilocarpine sweat testing measures chloride. In a person with compatible features, a result ≥60 mmol/L supports CF; intermediate results need repeat or further testing. Newborn screening is not diagnostic.

cards.front: IgA vasculitis (HSP): most common childhood vasculitis; triad of palpable [___] (buttocks/lower limbs), arthritis, abdominal pain; monitor for nephritis.
cards.context:
IgA vasculitis (HSP) is the commonest childhood vasculitis.

Mostly self-limiting; supportive care. Monitor renal function 6-12 months — long-term renal sequelae in 1-2%.

cards.front: First-line paediatric anaphylaxis: IM adrenaline 1:1000 at 0.01 mg/kg (capped at the adult dose) into the anterolateral thigh; repeat every [___] minutes if needed.
cards.context:
First-line for paediatric anaphylaxis is IM adrenaline 1:1000 at 0.01 mg/kg (max 0.5 mg) into lateral thigh. 1:1000 (1 mg/mL) is for IM — do NOT confuse with 1:10,000 (IV cardiac arrest dose).

EpiPen Jr (0.15 mg) for 7.5-20 kg, EpiPen (0.3 mg) for >20 kg. Repeat every 5 min if needed. IM-not-IV prevents catastrophic tachyarrhythmias.
